title: TikTok rolls out Likeness Detection globally, plus a public checker for AI-made videos

sources.name: TikTok Newsroom (en-GB): More tools to provide clarity and control around AI-generated content

kept.claim: TikTok has started rolling out Likeness Detection globally. It is an opt-in tool that helps eligible creators find and flag AI-generated content on TikTok that may use their likeness without consent.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'starting to globally roll out Likeness Detection, an opt-in tool...'. Source 0: 'started a global rollout'. Source 1 and Source 2 (AFP): global launch of its deepfake-detection tool for public figures. Source 2's text was only readable through its page metadata description; the article body was not in the fetched text.

kept.claim: The Likeness Detection rollout is gradual, not instant.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'with the tool gradually being rolled out'. Source 3: 'starting to globally roll out'.

kept.claim: Likeness Detection is available to eligible creators and public figures, including Government, Politician, or Political Party Accounts (GPPPAs).
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'available to eligible creators and public figures, including ... (GPPPAs)'. Source 0 quotes the same wording.

kept.claim: Likeness Detection works in three steps. Eligible creators verify their ID with a third-party partner. They are notified of content and accounts that may use their likeness and can review them in the tool. They can report content directly to TikTok's safety teams.
kept.evidence: Source 3 lists the three steps. Source 0 repeats them and says the partner was not named in the announcement.

kept.claim: Content that violates TikTok's community guidelines against harmful, misleading or nonconsensual depiction of private individuals will be removed.
kept.evidence: Source 3 step 3 states this. Source 0 quotes the newsroom post.

kept.claim: TikTok says Likeness Detection is designed to minimise data collection and preserve privacy, and TikTok does not keep ID documents.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'designed to minimise data collection and preserve privacy, and TikTok does not keep ID documents'. Source 0 says the same.

kept.claim: TikTok says it removes more than 99% of content that breaks its rules before anyone reports it. Anyone, whether or not they use TikTok, can report nonconsensual AI-generated content through its privacy reporting form.
kept.evidence: Source 3 and Source 0 (quoting the newsroom post) both state this.

kept.claim: TikTok launched a second tool, a public transparency checker. Anyone can upload an image or video to see whether it was generated or edited with TikTok's AI creation features, even without a TikTok account.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'People can upload an image or video to see whether it was generated or edited with TikTok's AI creation features, even if they don't have a TikTok account.' Source 0: 'Anyone can upload an image or video... without needing a TikTok account.'

kept.claim: The checker looks for C2PA Content Credentials and for VeraDura, TikTok's proprietary invisible watermark, which TikTok says is more durable and harder to remove.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'Alongside Content Credentials, the tool checks for VeraDura, our proprietary invisible watermark, which is more durable and harder to remove.' Source 0 says the same.

kept.claim: The checker detects content made or edited with TikTok's own AI tools. It is not a general-purpose AI detector.
kept.evidence: Source 3 limits the check to 'TikTok's AI creation features'. Source 0: 'only detects content made or edited with TikTok and ByteDance AI tools, so it is not a general-purpose AI detector'. The 'not general-purpose' wording is in Source 0 only.

kept.claim: TikTok says its AI labelling tools and technologies have helped it label over/more than 5 billion AI-generated videos on its platform to date. This is a cumulative total.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'helped us label over 5 billion AI-generated videos on our platform to date'. Source 0: 'more than 5 billion'.

kept.claim: TikTok says it became the first video platform to adopt C2PA Content Credentials, in 2024, and automatically adds them to AI-generated content made with its tools.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'In 2024, we became the first video platform to adopt C2PA Content Credentials...'. Source 0 says the same.

kept.claim: TikTok says its in-app AI literacy hub, launched in July, has helped more than 4 million people learn to spot AI-generated content.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'launched in July, has helped more than 4 million people'. Source 0 says the same.

kept.claim: TikTok is a member of the C2PA Steering Committee. Source 0 adds that it joined in July.
kept.evidence: Source 3: 'As members of the C2PA Steering Committee...'. Source 0: 'joined the C2PA Steering Committee in July'. The July detail is in Source 0 only.

kept.claim: TikTok announced the tool at its safety and innovation event or forum in London.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'said at TikTok's safety and innovation event in London'. Source 0: 'Safety and Innovation Forum in London'.

kept.claim: The tool is positioned against AI-generated disinformation ahead of a wave of European elections next year. Source 0 gives the year as 2027. Source 1 names Italy, France and Greece.
kept.evidence: Source 1 and Source 2 (AFP): 'ahead of a wave of European elections next year'. Source 0: 'a wave of elections across Europe in 2027'. Only Source 1 names Italy, France and Greece.

kept.claim: Francesca Scapolo, TikTok's Government Relations Lead for European Elections, said the tool would help politicians and government identify potentially AI-generated content shared potentially without their consent.
kept.evidence: Source 1 quotes her directly. Source 0 paraphrases her and credits AFP.

kept.claim: TikTok is owned by China-based ByteDance.
kept.evidence: Source 1: 'TikTok, owned by China-based ByteDance'. Source 0 calls ByteDance TikTok's parent.

dropped.claim: AFP describes the Likeness Detection tool as aimed at politicians and accounts with a large number of followers.
dropped.evidence: Source 1: 'allows politicians and accounts with a large number of followers on TikTok to find and report AI-generated content using their image without consent'.

dropped.claim: The checker also recognizes AI features in four ByteDance apps: CapCut, Dreamina, Hypic and Pippit.
dropped.evidence: Source 0 states this. The TikTok newsroom post does not mention these apps.

dropped.claim: The checker is available now via TikTok's Transparency Centre.
dropped.evidence: Source 3: 'The tool is available now via our Transparency Centre.'

dropped.claim: The cumulative labelled-video figure was more than 3 billion in July and more than 1.3 billion in November 2025.
Date version A: the TikTok newsroom post announcing both tools is dated November 20, 2026.
Date version B: MBW says TikTok announced the global rollout on Thursday (November 19) at its Safety and Innovation Forum in London.
dropped.evidence: Source 0: 'announced the global rollout on Thursday (November 19) at its Safety and Innovation Forum in London'. Source 0 also says the checker was unveiled on November 19.

dropped.claim: Date version C: AFP, as carried by CTV, says TikTok announced the launch on Friday. Source 2 was published 2026-11-20, which is a Friday. RTÉ published the same AFP story at 2026-11-20 05:40 UTC and does not name a weekday in its text.
dropped.evidence: Source 2 metadata description: 'TikTok announced Friday the global launch of its deepfake-detection tool for public figures'.

dropped.claim: The announcement is not the start of the tool. TikTok began testing Likeness Detection with a small group of creators in the United States in July. Identity checks in that test were run by Jumio using a real-time selfie and a government ID check.
dropped.evidence: Source 0 states this, citing its own earlier reporting. The TikTok newsroom post does not mention the July test or Jumio.
